THOUGHT: This 10-month-old boy presents with recurrent stridor and wheezing—upper airway obstruction symptoms—not typical of reactive airway disease or viral bronchiolitis, which usually present with cough, rhinorrhea, and lower respiratory signs. The positional and activity-related pattern is highly suggestive of dynamic airway compression: worsening with crying (increased intrathoracic pressure and airway narrowing), feeding (esophageal distension and proximity to compressed trachea), and neck flexion (which further narrows an already compromised tracheal lumen), with relief on neck extension (which pulls the trachea anteriorly and may alleviate compression). Vomiting post-feeding suggests concomitant esophageal compression causing dysphagia and gastroesophageal reflux–like symptoms. Physical exam shows mild intercostal retractions (indicating increased work of breathing) and wheezing without crackles or fever—arguing against infection or parenchymal lung disease. Crucially, imaging confirms a double aortic arch: a complete vascular ring where both right and left aortic arches persist, encircling and compressing the trachea and esophagus. This is the most common symptomatic vascular ring and classically presents in infancy with stridor, wheeze, dysphagia, and feeding difficulties—exactly matching this case. Other diagnoses (e.g., laryngomalacia, tracheomalacia, asthma, GERD alone) do not explain the triad of tracheal + esophageal compression confirmed by imaging, nor the characteristic positional exacerbation and radiographic findings.

DIAGNOSIS: Double aortic arch
